title: The Allocator Role is held by a contract, not by the multisigs that actually use it
content:
A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.2.3 states the Allocator Role (`ALLOCATOR_ROLE`) "is held by the AdministeredAgent contract, with the Relayer Multisigs registered as its Actors... and submitting operations through it." A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.2.4 defines an Actor as an address registered on the AdministeredAgent authorized to submit allocation operations to the Controller *through* that role — with the Relayer Multisigs of both a Prime Agent and the Core Operator registered.

This is a deliberate layer of indirection. The privileged position in the access-control contract is occupied by a contract whose internal registry decides who may exercise it. Operator turnover, key rotation and emergency removal all become writes to that registry instead of grant/revoke calls on the Instance's access-control contract.

Two capabilities fall out of the indirection. It is what allows the Revoker to eject one operator without disturbing the role (A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.2.5), and it is what lets *multiple* independent parties — a Prime Agent's relayers and the Core Operator's — share one role slot with individually revocable access.

The cost is a second permission surface: the AdministeredAgent's own Admin/Grantor/Actor/Revoker configuration must be governed as carefully as the role it fronts, or the indirection becomes the weakest link rather than a containment boundary.
description: Relayer Multisigs are registered as Actors on an AdministeredAgent that holds ALLOCATOR_ROLE, so changing operators is an Actor-registry edit rather than a role grant on the access-control contract.
